linger:A terrace on the Place Carnot.name: A terrace on the Place Carnot
linger:A terrace on the Place Carnot.teaser: Beaune's living room: a chair on the square, a coffee, and the whole town walking past
linger:A terrace on the Place Carnot.story: Place Carnot is where Beaune crosses itself. The commercial heart of the walled town, it runs into the Place de la Halle, so on market mornings the stalls spill toward its edges and in summer a brocante takes over the paving. Around it: Mulot & Petitjean selling Dijon pain d'épices at number 1, Alain Hess's cheese counter, the starred Le Carmin. Sit on a terrace with a coffee and you see the day's traffic go by: shoppers with baskets, cellar staff on their way to work, tour groups heading for the Hôtel-Dieu one block on.
linger:A terrace on the Place Carnot.why: Come for a morning coffee and the people-watching, not for wine: the terrace pours are covered by the skip card on Burgundy by the glass.
facts: Place Carnot, inside the ramparts, one block from the Hôtel-Dieu

linger:Athenaeum de la Vigne et du Vin.name: Athenaeum de la Vigne et du Vin
linger:Athenaeum de la Vigne et du Vin.teaser: A bookshop given over to the vine, across the street from the Hôtel-Dieu's glazed roof
linger:Athenaeum de la Vigne et du Vin.story: Step out of the Hôtel-Dieu and the Athenaeum is facing you on rue de l'Hôtel-Dieu: shelves of books about wine and almost nothing else, from the standard Burgundy references to vintage guides and cookbooks, with glassware, tastevins, corkscrews and cellar tools beside them. This is where to buy the map of the climats that makes the slope west of town readable before you walk it. The shop also pours wine to taste on the spot and in 2025 staged evenings of wine and theatre under the name Vignobles en scène.

drink:Pinot Noir.name: Pinot Noir
drink:Pinot Noir.teaser: One grape for the whole red Côte, and a different wine every few hundred metres of slope
drink:Pinot Noir.story: Every red of the Côte d'Or worth its name is Pinot Noir. The grape stays the same; what changes is the ground. Beaune's own appellation is mostly red, and its premier crus climb the slope just behind the town: Les Grèves, Les Bressandes, Les Teurons, Champs Pimont. Taste two of them side by side and the lesson of Burgundy arrives in the glass: a thin-skinned grape that shows the soil, the slope and the exposure more than it shows itself. Young Beaune smells of red cherry and raspberry; with age it turns to earth, leaves and spice.
drink:Pinot Noir.why: Order two Beaune premier crus from neighbouring climats by the glass and taste the slope change.
facts: Pale to mid ruby, red cherry and raspberry when young, forest floor and spice with age; light tannin, fresh acidity
Bourgogne, then village (Beaune, Pommard, Volnay), then Beaune 1er Cru with the climat named: Les Grèves, Les Bressandes, Les Teurons

drink:Chardonnay and the Clos des Mouche.name: Chardonnay and the Clos des Mouches
drink:Chardonnay and the Clos des Mouche.teaser: The benchmark white grape, and the one Beaune premier cru that made its name in white
drink:Chardonnay and the Clos des Mouche.story: A short drive south of the ramparts, Meursault and Puligny-Montrachet turned Chardonnay into the standard every dry white is measured against; north, Corton-Charlemagne does the same on the hill of Corton. Beaune itself is red country with one famous white exception: the Clos des Mouches, a premier cru on the slope toward Pommard. Joseph Drouhin owns the largest share, 14 of its roughly 25 hectares, planted half Chardonnay and half Pinot Noir, and Decanter has marked a century of the house's wine from it. The white is the bottle that put the name on lists.
drink:Chardonnay and the Clos des Mouche.why: Ask for the Drouhin Clos des Mouches blanc: Beaune's one white with a world reputation.
facts: Pale gold, lemon, white peach and hazelnut, a buttery or toasted note from barrel

drink:The climat.name: The climat
drink:The climat.teaser: 42 premier crus and not one grand cru: why Beaune's slope is read parcel by parcel
drink:The climat.story: A climat is a named, mapped plot of vines whose wine has been tasted and judged as distinct for centuries: the work of monks, dukes and growers who kept walking the same rows. When UNESCO inscribed the Climats of Burgundy on 4 July 2015, the site took in 1,247 of them along the Côte from Dijon to the Maranges. Beaune's own appellation counts 42 climats ranked premier cru, running in a band from the Pommard border to Savigny, and no grand cru at all. Read the system first at the Cité des Climats et Vins, then walk up behind the ramparts.
drink:The climat.why: Learn three climat names before your first tasting; every Burgundy label then starts to make sense.
facts: The same grape from neighbouring climats tastes different: that difference is the point
Commune, then rank, then climat: Beaune 1er Cru Les Grèves; a grand cru shows only the climat, as in Corton

drink:Kir.name: Kir
drink:Kir.teaser: A measure of Dijon cassis under cold Aligoté, named for the priest who was mayor of Dijon
drink:Kir.story: Félix Kir, canon of the Church, Resistance figure and mayor of Dijon from 1945 to 1968, served white wine and blackcurrant liqueur at every reception, and the drink took his name. The liqueur is Dijon's own: the town's crème de cassis was first made in 1841 by Denis Lagoute, who macerated blackcurrants cold in alcohol. Today Cassis de Dijon is a geographical indication with rules, approved in 2013: made within Dijon, at least 400 g of sugar a litre and 15 percent alcohol, with Noir de Bourgogne or Royal de Naples berries in the mix. One part of it to four or five of sharp Aligoté.
drink:Kir.why: Order a Kir before dinner with gougères: the Aligoté's acidity keeps the cassis from cloying.
facts: Deep pink to garnet, blackcurrant over lemony white wine; sweet then sharp
Bourgogne Aligoté for the wine; Cassis de Dijon or Crème de cassis de Bourgogne for the liqueur

drink:Crémant de Bourgogne.name: Crémant de Bourgogne
drink:Crémant de Bourgogne.teaser: Bottle-fermented like Champagne, an appellation since October 1975, poured at any hour
drink:Crémant de Bourgogne.story: Crémant de Bourgogne became an appellation by decree on 17 October 1975, the same day as Crémant de Loire, and the producers marked its fiftieth year in 2025. It is made the way Champagne is: a second fermentation in the bottle, then at least nine months resting on the lees before disgorgement. The longer-aged tiers say so on the label, Éminent at 24 months and Grand Éminent at 36. Chardonnay and Pinot Noir lead the blend, with Aligoté and Gamay allowed. It is the honest bubble of Burgundy at a fraction of the price, and the base of a Kir Royale.
drink:Crémant de Bourgogne.why: Ask for an Éminent or Grand Éminent bottling: the extra time on the lees shows in the glass.
facts: Fine bubbles, green apple, lemon and brioche; rosé versions with red berries

drink:Marc and Fine de Bourgogne.name: Marc and Fine de Bourgogne
drink:Marc and Fine de Bourgogne.teaser: Two Burgundy brandies: one from the pressed skins, one from the lees left in the barrel
drink:Marc and Fine de Bourgogne.story: After the harvest, nothing is wasted. Marc de Bourgogne is distilled from what remains in the press, the skins, seeds and stalks, then aged at least two years in wood. Fine de Bourgogne comes from wine still carrying its fine lees, drawn off when the barrels are racked, and needs at least three years in oak: rounder, softer, more like a small Cognac. Both are bottled at 40 percent or more. The names were protected in the 1940s; the current appellations rest on decrees of March 2011. Marc is also the spirit that washes the rind of Époisses.
drink:Marc and Fine de Bourgogne.why: End a Beaune dinner with a Fine: smoother than the Marc, and rarer on a list.
facts: Marc: amber, grape skin, dried fruit and heat; Fine: rounder, vanilla, oak and dried apricot

bars:Marché aux Vins.name: Marché aux Vins
bars:Marché aux Vins.teaser: A self-guided tasting through the chapels and cellars of the old Cordeliers church
bars:Marché aux Vins.story: Opposite the Hôtel-Dieu, the Marché aux Vins pours inside the former church of the Cordeliers, the Franciscan friars of Beaune. You take a tastevin and walk at your own pace through the cool stone cellars and the Gothic chapels above, tasting as you go: five wines, one of them a premier cru, in about forty minutes on the basic route. Arrive at the 10:00 opening on a weekday and you have the vaults nearly to yourself, the stone still cold, the only sound the wine going into the cup. The chapels also hang an art gallery you can see free from the shop.
bars:Marché aux Vins.why: Be at the door at 10:00 on a weekday, before the groups arrive.

bars:Bouchard Père & Fils.name: Bouchard Père & Fils
bars:Bouchard Père & Fils.teaser: A wine house in the towers Louis XI built to hold Beaune down, its bottles 10 m underground
bars:Bouchard Père & Fils.story: In 1478 Beaune rose against Louis XI; the king besieged it, the town gave in on 2 July, and he ordered a fortress to keep it in line. The Château de Beaune was finished only in 1527, long after his death. Four of its five towers still stand on the ramparts, listed since 1937. Bernard Bouchard, of a house founded in 1731, bought it in 1820, and Bouchard Père & Fils has aged its premier and grand crus in the galleries beneath ever since, up to 10 metres down, among more than 2,000 bottles from the 19th century.
bars:Bouchard Père & Fils.why: Book well ahead: this is an appointment visit, and the reason to go is to stand inside Louis XI's rampart.
facts: Château de Beaune, 15 rue du Château, on the north-east ramparts

bars:Patriarche Père & Fils.name: Patriarche Père & Fils
bars:Patriarche Père & Fils.teaser: Five kilometres of galleries under an old Visitandine convent, walked alone with a tastevin
bars:Patriarche Père & Fils.story: Jean-Baptiste Patriarche founded his wine house in Beaune in 1780, and on 23 August 1796 he bought the former convent of the Visitandine nuns, which the house still occupies. In the 20th century André Boisseaux joined some 35 neighbouring cellars into one network, now about 5 kilometres of dim vaulted galleries holding, the house says, around two million bottles: Patriarche calls them the largest cellars in Burgundy. You walk them on your own, with video points in several languages, past walls of dusty bottles in the cold, and finish with six wines poured by a sommelier.
bars:Patriarche Père & Fils.why: Of all Beaune's cellars, this walk shows best how much wine lies under the town's streets.
facts: 5-7 rue du Collège, inside the ramparts
